name: Dulsyn
description: A targeted sensory dampening compound that attenuates the haptic and proprioceptive feedback signals transmitted between chrome and the organic nervous system, reducing augment sensitivity to near-zero. Prescribed legitimately for patients experiencing hyperesthesia after new augment installation — the overwhelming sensory flood of suddenly having a robot arm that feels everything — and for individuals with augment-related chronic pain. On the street, it's used recreationally by people who want to feel nothing through their chrome, and tactically by operators who need to function through catastrophic augment damage without the pain signal shutting them down.
effects: Augment haptic and proprioceptive feedback reduced 80-100%
Psychological dissociation from chrome — augments feel like tools rather than body parts
Useful for surgical augment work without full anesthesia
side_effects: Loss of fine motor feedback — precision tasks with chrome become difficult
Psychological distress from body dissociation in some users
Risk of augment damage going unnoticed (no pain warning)
Rebound hyperesthesia on come-down — augments become agonizingly sensitive
Long-term use associated with permanent reduction in augment-nerve integration quality
cultural_context: In Tier 2-3 clinics, Dulsyn is considered a humane necessity — the first weeks after major augmentation are often described as sensory torture, and Novafold's version has a solid safety record. The street use splits into two camps: people who use it to cope with the psychological burden of feeling like a machine (a surprisingly common mental health crisis among heavily augmented individuals), and hard operators who take it before a fight so that losing fingers or taking augment damage doesn't slow them down. The rebound sensitivity on come-down is considered a feature by some — a few hours of exquisitely heightened touch sensation after the numbness breaks.
story_hooks: A Tier 3 office worker with full-arm chrome has become dependent on Dulsyn to get through her workday — without it, the constant sensory input from her augments is unbearable, but her dosage is escalating and the rebound crashes are getting worse each cycle.

An operator took Dulsyn before a job and didn't feel his augmented leg fail catastrophically mid-run — he completed the job, but the leg is now unsalvageable, and the fixer who supplied the drug may have done so intentionally.

Novafold is quietly recalling a batch of Dulsyn after discovering it was contaminated during manufacturing — the contaminated batch doesn't just dampen augment sensitivity, it appears to permanently sever specific haptic nerve pathways.
